title: Studying in South Korea: GKS and university admissions
summary: How the Global Korea Scholarship embassy and university tracks differ, what to check in each year's notice, and how university admission works separately from the scholarship.

sources.title: Study in Korea: official portal (GKS notices)

review_note: Only the Study in Korea homepage was reachable at check time; the GKS notice and university pages returned 404 and the English homepage returned 404. No GKS amounts, quotas, dates or country lists are stated. The article tells the reader to use the current year's official notice for those. Track descriptions (embassy and university) come from aggregator summaries and should be confirmed on the official notice before publication.
body:
## In short

- The Global Korea Scholarship (GKS) is the Korean government's scholarship for international undergraduate students. It is run through the Study in Korea portal.
- GKS is a separate application from university admission. Some students apply to GKS through a Korean embassy and others apply through a participating university. The two routes have different timelines.
- Each year's guidelines set the eligibility rules, the deadlines and the benefits. Read the notice for the intake you are applying for.
- For a university without a scholarship, the admission rules are set by the university. Language tests and document rules apply in both cases.

## What GKS is

GKS is funded by the Korean government and aims to bring international students to study in Korea. The undergraduate track is for students who want a bachelor's degree at a Korean university. Applicants are selected in a competitive process, and places are limited by the quota in each year's guidelines.

Read the official notice for the year before you do anything else. Previous years' summaries often list benefits or deadlines that no longer apply. The Study in Korea portal is the place to find the current notice, the application forms and the list of participating universities.

## The two tracks

**Embassy track.** You submit your application to the Korean embassy in your home country, which runs its own selection. The embassy track is usually the route for students who do not yet have an offer from a university.

**University track.** You apply directly to a participating Korean university, and the university selects students for the scholarship. Deadlines depend on the university, so you may have to apply to several to improve your chances.

Check which track your target university uses. Some universities run both, and it is possible to apply through both if the notice allows it. Read the rule on that before you submit.

## Eligibility

Eligibility rules typically cover nationality, age, previous education and health. Many notices require that you have not already completed a bachelor's degree, and some have age limits. Check whether your country is on the list of partner countries for the year you are applying for. Do not assume that a neighbouring country has the same rule.

## Language requirements

Korean-taught programmes usually require a Korean language test, such as TOPIK. Many GKS places include a language training year before the degree begins, so you may not need a test score at the start. Read the notice for the language level expected at the start of your degree. English-taught programmes usually ask for an English test instead.

## Admission to a Korean university

Admission and scholarship are separate decisions. Even if your GKS application is strong, you must still meet the university's admission requirements. Typical items include:

- A school transcript and graduation certificate, often with an official translation.
- An application form and a personal statement, which the university may ask for in Korean or English.
- A language test result, as set by the programme.
- A recommendation letter or a letter from your school, depending on the university.
- Any entrance exam or interview that the university runs.

Check whether the university requires the documents to be apostilled or legalised, and ask early, because the process takes time.

## The timeline

Use the current notice for exact dates, but the general pattern for an autumn start is:

- Late in the year before entry: read the notice and shortlist universities.
- Early in the new year: prepare documents, language results and the statement.
- Mid-year: submit the embassy track application or the university application, depending on your route.
- Later in the year: wait for results, then confirm the offer and visa steps.

Do not rely on this pattern to set dates. The official notice sets the real deadlines, and they can differ for each university.

## Living in Korea

Scholarship benefits may cover some living costs, but you should still check what they include. Ask whether housing is provided, whether there is a monthly allowance, and whether it is paid during language training. Plan for costs that a scholarship may not cover, such as local phone plans, personal travel and any extra course materials.

## Common mistakes

- Applying to the wrong track or to a university that does not take part.
- Using an old notice for a different year.
- Missing a document, such as a translation or a legalised copy.
- Treating the scholarship as a guarantee of admission.
- Ignoring the language requirement until the last month.

## Choosing a university in Korea

Korean universities differ in their language of instruction, their subjects and their location. Some have large international programmes, while others teach mainly in Korean. Check the list of programmes the university offers in English, the number of international students, and whether the university takes part in GKS. A university that participates in the scholarship will publish its own GKS page or notice.

Visit the university's website and read the admissions pages for international applicants. Look for the application calendar, the document list, and the language rule for your programme. If the site is only in Korean, use the international office's email address to ask for an English version of the notice.

## Studying Korean

Korean language skills matter for daily life even in English-taught programmes. Many students take a language course at the start, and some universities provide one as part of the scholarship package. Ask whether a language course is included in the scholarship, how long it lasts, and what level you need at the end of it to start your degree.

Practise Korean before you arrive if you can. Basic reading and survival phrases help with transport, housing and health appointments. Many students find that the first months are the hardest, so plan some time for adjustment and for the bureaucracy of registration.

## Health, housing and daily life

International students in Korea are usually asked to register their residence and to arrange health insurance. Ask the international office early about dormitory places, which are often allocated through an application. If you rent privately, check the deposit rules and the contract language, and ask a Korean-speaking friend or the international office to read it with you.

Public transport in Korean cities is reliable and affordable, and a transport card covers most trips. Plan a monthly budget that includes food, phone, transport, books and small social costs. Keep a record of your spending for the first two months to see where the money goes.

## Keeping your place

Scholarship holders are usually required to keep a minimum academic standard and to follow the rules of the programme. Read the conditions in your award letter, and keep copies of your grades and attendance records. If your situation changes, such as a serious illness or a family emergency, contact the international office at once, because the rules often allow for special cases if you raise them early.

## Checklist

- [ ] Read the current GKS notice on the Study in Korea portal.
- [ ] Confirm that your country is a partner country for the intake.
- [ ] Choose the embassy track or the university track, and check the deadlines.
- [ ] Confirm the language requirement for your programme.
- [ ] Prepare certified transcripts and translations.
- [ ] Ask each university whether apostille or legalisation is required.
- [ ] Keep a backup plan in case the scholarship is not awarded.
